question.:question/problem:
Consider the matrices

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that two matrices are inverses when their products in both orders equal $I_2$.

Which statements are true? Choose the correct combination.

I. $B$ is an inverse of $A$

II. $BC=CB=I_2$

III. $CA=AC=I_2$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use row-column multiplication and compare with $I_2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}AB&=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0 & 1\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1 \\ 0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & 0\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}BA&=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0 & 1\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot 1 \\ 0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & 0\cdot 2+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Both products equal $I_2$, so $B$ is an inverse of $A$.

$$
\begin{aligned}BC&=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0 & 1\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot 1 \\ 0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & 0\cdot 3+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In $BC$, the entry in row $1$, column $2$ is $1$, whereas the identity entry is $0$. This mismatch proves that $C$ is not an inverse of $B$. One failing product suffices to reject the pair.

$$
\begin{aligned}CA&=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot 1+3\cdot 0 & 1\cdot 2+3\cdot 1 \\ 0\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & 0\cdot 2+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In $CA$, the entry in row $1$, column $2$ is $5$, whereas the identity entry is $0$. This mismatch proves that $A$ is not an inverse of $C$. One failing product suffices to reject the pair.

The statement $B$ is an inverse of $A$ is **true**.

The statement $BC=CB=I_2$ is **false**.

The statement $CA=AC=I_2$ is **false**.

The correct combination is I only.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$, with columns in the order $x,y,z$:

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & -1 & -1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Keeping the columns in the order $x,y,z$, the augmented matrix is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & -1 & -1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

Normalize the first pivot with $R_1\leftarrow (-1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The matrix is in row echelon form. There is one pivot. The two zero rows express $0=0$, so they impose no restrictions. The **basic variable** is $y$; the **free variables** are $x,z$. The remaining equation and its rearrangement are

$$
\begin{aligned}y+z &=4 \\ y &=4-z\end{aligned}
$$

Thus all solutions are

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 4-z \\ z\end{bmatrix},\quad x,z\in\mathbb{R}
$$

Separating the constant part and the contributions of the two free variables gives

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+x\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+z\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\quad x,z\in\mathbb{R}
$$

The two free parameters range independently over all real numbers, so the solution set is a plane.

The matrices $B$ and $A$ differ in just one entry. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -3 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -3 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero. A singular matrix has no multiplicative inverse; a nonsingular square matrix has one. Compare both determinants rather than assuming that one changed entry changes singularity.

Expand along the top row, with signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(B) &= (-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +3\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -3 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\
&= (-1)\left(-2-(3)\right) \\
&\quad +3\left(4-(3)\right) \\
&\quad +(-2)\left(6-(-3)\right) \\
&= (-1)\cdot (-5) \\
&\quad +3\cdot 1 \\
&\quad +(-2)\cdot 9 \\
&= 5+3-18 \\
&= -10
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(A) &= (-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +3\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\
&= (-1)\left(-2-(3)\right) \\
&\quad +3\left(4-(1)\right) \\
&\quad +(-2)\left(6-(-1)\right) \\
&= (-1)\cdot (-5) \\
&\quad +3\cdot 3 \\
&\quad +(-2)\cdot 7 \\
&= 5+9-14 \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(B)=-10\ne0$, $B$ is **not** singular.

Since $\det(A)=0$, $A$ is singular.

Do not select “$B$ and $A$ either both have multiplicative inverses or both have no multiplicative inverse.”

Do not select “$A$ is **not** a singular matrix.”

Do not select “$B$ is a singular matrix.”

Select “$\det(B)=-10$.”

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $B$ and $A$ either both have multiplicative inverses or both have no multiplicative inverse

question.:question/problem:
Consider the matrices
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
Recall that $B=A^{-1}$ means $AB=BA=I_3$. Which of the following statements are true? Use direct verification. Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Check $B$. The entry in row $1$, column $3$ already disproves the identity claim:

$$
\begin{aligned}(AB)_{13}&=(1)(2)+(0)(0)+(-1)(1) \\ &=1\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $AB\ne I_3$, so $B$ is not an inverse of $A$. One mismatching entry is enough to reject a candidate.

The statement $B\ne A^{-1}$ is **true** by the product test above.

Select $B\ne A^{-1}$.
